parakeet: The skid started the controversy. The false aftermath distorted how the controversy was understood. At that point, people are no longer only responding to what happened. That matters a lot for the secular community because this is exactly the kind of environment where people who pride themselves on skepticism can still get played. But when people in skeptical spaces start repeating false information, circulating unverified claims, and building commentary around things that were never actually confirmed, then the problem is no longer just look how irrational they are. It becomes a question of whether our communities are really committed to evidence when the story is emotionally satisfying, or only when skepticism costs us nothing. And that's where the windmill problem comes in. Because once false information gets enough traction, people start preparing to battle the fiction it created. They start arguing against fake responses. They start condemning fallout that never happened. They start positioning themselves against an invented version of events as though they are doing serious cultural analysis, when in reality they're shadow boxing with the narrative the internet assembled. It means a person can be directionally right about a broader issue and still be intellectually sloppy in how they engage a specific event. And if that becomes normal, then the secular community risks becoming just another space where confidence outruns verification. What troubles me most is that this kind of thing can make people feel informed when they're actually being manipulated. It gives them the feeling of clarity, the feeling of righteousness, the feeling of being on the side of reason and having the moral high ground while quietly severing them from the hard work of checking what is true. And once a community starts rewarding that pattern, it becomes easier and easier for bad information to pass through simply because it flatters the audience's instincts. That is how skepticism degrades. Not all at once, and not usually through some dramatic betrayal of principle, but through a hundred moments where people decide that a satisfying narrative is good enough. It's about what happens when even communities built on doubt, evidence, and critical thinking become vulnerable to the emotional momentum of a story. If we're not careful, we'll end up doing exactly what we claim to resist: spreading false information, reacting before verifying, and gearing up to fight windmills the internet created.
